p: Alexander Pope, the poet, wrote an epitaph for Sir Isaac Newton which every English schoolboy knows: Nature and Nature's laws lay hid in night; God said, Let Newton be! and all was light. It is a fine couplet and a gross exaggeration, as epitaphs are entitled to be. Newton himself, in a more modest mood, wrote to his rival Robert Hooke that if he had seen further, it was by standing on the shoulders of giants. The story of how he came to stand there, between the years fifteen forty-three and sixteen eighty-seven, is the story of what the men of the twentieth century called the Scientific Revolution, the most important change in the way men think since the Greeks.

Before it, the educated men of Europe understood the world chiefly through the writings of Aristotle, as interpreted by the scholars of the Middle Ages, and of the astronomer Ptolemy of Alexandria. The earth stood motionless at the centre of the universe. Around it, carried upon nested crystal spheres, turned the moon, the sun, the planets and the fixed stars. Everything beneath the moon was made of four elements, earth, water, air and fire, and was subject to change and decay; everything above the moon was made of a fifth element, perfect and unchanging, and moved in perfect circles. Heavy things fell because it was their nature to seek the centre of the universe. It was a coherent, beautiful and, in its way, reasonable picture, fitting both the evidence of the senses and the teachings of the Church. It was also wrong.

In fifteen forty-three, as he lay dying, a canon of the cathedral of Frombork in Poland, Nicolaus Copernicus, received the first printed copy of his book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, in which he proposed that the sun, not the earth, stands at the centre, and that the earth turns daily upon its axis and travels yearly around the sun. He had held the idea for decades and hesitated to publish it. It was not at first much more accurate than Ptolemy's system, and it contradicted common sense: if the earth moves, why do we not feel it? Why are we not flung off?

The Danish nobleman Tycho Brahe, from his observatory on an island in the Sound, made observations of the planets more accurate than any before, without a telescope. His assistant, the German Johannes Kepler, laboured for years over Tycho's observations of the planet Mars, and found, in sixteen hundred and nine, that the planets move not in circles but in ellipses, that is, in ovals, with the sun at one focus, and that they move faster when nearer to the sun. It was the first time that the motions of the heavens had been described by exact laws derived from measurement.

In Italy, Galileo Galilei, a professor of mathematics at Padua, heard of a Dutch invention, the telescope, made one himself, and in sixteen-ten turned it upon the sky. He saw mountains on the moon, which therefore was no perfect sphere; spots upon the sun; countless stars invisible to the naked eye; and four moons circling the planet Jupiter, which showed that not everything in the heavens circles the earth. He was also the founder of the modern science of motion: he showed, by rolling balls down inclined planes and timing them, that falling bodies accelerate at a constant rate, regardless of their weight, if the resistance of the air is set aside. The story that he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa is told by his first biographer and may be true; the experiments that mattered were done more quietly.

Galileo argued for the system of Copernicus with such brilliance, and such contempt for his opponents, that he was summoned before the Roman Inquisition in sixteen thirty-three, forced to abjure the doctrine on his knees, and confined to his house for the rest of his life. The story that he muttered as he rose, and yet it moves, appears first more than a century later, and is very probably a legend. It deserves to be true.

Alongside the discoveries came arguments about how knowledge should be got. Francis Bacon in England urged that men should cease to rely on the authority of ancient books and should instead gather facts by observation and experiment, patiently, and reason upward from them. René Descartes in France urged that men should doubt everything that could be doubted, and rebuild knowledge from certain foundations by mathematical reasoning. The new science combined the two: experiment and mathematics. In London, in sixteen-sixty, a group of gentlemen founded a society for the improvement of natural knowledge, which King Charles the Second chartered as the Royal Society. Its motto is a Latin phrase, nullius in verba, which means, roughly, take nobody's word for it. That is the whole of the scientific method in four words.

Isaac Newton was born on Christmas Day sixteen forty-two, in Lincolnshire, a premature and sickly baby, after his father's death. He was a solitary, suspicious, quarrelsome man of supreme genius. In sixteen sixty-five and sixty-six, when the University of Cambridge was closed by the plague, he went home to his mother's farm and, in some eighteen months, laid the foundations of the calculus, discovered that white light is a mixture of all the colours, and began to think about gravity. The story of the apple, which he told in old age, is very likely true in substance: he saw an apple fall and wondered whether the force that drew it to the earth might reach as far as the moon.

In sixteen eighty-seven, urged and financed by the astronomer Edmond Halley, he published the Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, usually called by the first word of its Latin title, the Principia. In it he set out three laws of motion, of which the first says that a body continues at rest or in uniform motion unless a force acts upon it, and the law of universal gravitation: that every particle of matter in the universe attracts every other with a force that grows weaker as the square of the distance between them grows. From these few principles he showed that he could derive Kepler's laws of the planets, the motions of the moon, the tides of the sea, the paths of comets and the flattening of the earth at its poles. The fall of an apple and the course of the planets were the same thing. The heavens and the earth obeyed the same laws, and the laws could be written in mathematics.

Newton spent his later years as Master of the Mint, hunting down counterfeiters with great zeal and having them hanged, and as President of the Royal Society, quarrelling with Leibniz over which of them had invented the calculus. He spent more of his time on the interpretation of the prophecies of Daniel and on alchemy than on physics; the economist John Maynard Keynes, who bought his private papers in the twentieth century, wrote that Newton was not the first of the age of reason, but the last of the magicians. He died in seventeen twenty-seven and was buried in Westminster Abbey, where the French philosopher Voltaire, watching, observed that England honoured a mathematician as other nations honour a king.

The Scientific Revolution did not merely add to knowledge. It changed the idea of knowledge. It taught that the universe is governed by regular laws, that those laws can be discovered by observation, experiment and mathematics, and that no authority, however ancient or sacred, may overrule the evidence. Every engine of my own century, every railway and telegraph, rests on that foundation. So, the Encyclopaedia assures me, does everything that follows.
